newsitem.title: CANADA: Air Canada up on Canadian troubles.
newsitem.headline: Air Canada up on Canadian troubles.

text.p: Shares of Air Canada rose sharply on Monday as investors appeared to shun troubled Canadian Airlines Corp stock in favor of the financially stronger Montreal-based carrier, analysts said.
Air Canada was up 0.50 to 5.85 on the Toronto Stock Exchange in third most active volume of more than 1.5 million shares.
By contrast, shares of Canadian Airlines fell 0.36 to 1.25 on more than 183,000 shares in Toronto.
Analysts said Air Canada was up mainly because of renewed interest in the carrier and disenchantment with financially troubled Canadian Airlines.

On Friday, Canadian announced a four-year C$800 million restructuring plan that ncluded a wage-cut proposal quickly rejected by its biggest union. Canadian said its 1996 loss would be "significant," although the shortfall was expected to be lower than the carrier's C$195 million loss in 1995.
Jacques Kavafian, analyst at Research Capital, said Monday's move in the two airline stocks was related to Canadian's misfortunes and Air Canada's growing financial strength.
"Basically, it's a combination of Canadian's restructuring announcement on Friday and people having time to reflect on it," Kavafian said.
"Air Canada has a lot of money and is a real company. Canadian is in restructuring mode," he said.
Kavafian expected Air Canada to earn C$0.35 a share, before one-time gains in 1996, and C$0.80 a share before gains in 1997.
Including gains, Air Canada was expected to earn C$1.10 a share this year and C$1.75 a share next year, he said.

Air Canada's expected net profit this year, before gains on the sale of its 22 percent stake in Continental Airlines Inc, would be its first "real profit" in several years, said Kavafian, which is attracting renewed interest from investors.

Although Canadian Airlines' restructing plans do not include any pullback from passenger service in the Montreal-Toronto-Ottawa triangle, analysts have been expecting the carrier to withdraw from that market, which is dominated by Air Canada.
Durrett said last week he expected Canadian to maintain its service in the Montreal-Toronto-Ottawa market.
